You complained to the city about the mold, and the increase came three days after the inspection. Your neighbors' rent stayed the same. Those facts point toward retaliation. DETAILS

### Does Florida law protect you from retaliation for a code complaint?
Yes. Under s. 83.64(1)(a), a landlord may not "discriminatorily increase a tenant's rent" primarily because the tenant "complained to a governmental agency charged with responsibility for enforcement of a building, housing, or health code of a suspected violation applicable to the premises." Your April 28 complaint to city code enforcement fits that description. Your lease is a month-to-month lease in a private apartment building, so the chapter covers you.

### Does the different treatment of your neighbors matter?
Yes. Section 83.64(4) says "discrimination" means being "treated differently as to the rent charged." The statute makes that "a prerequisite to a finding of retaliatory conduct." You say two neighbors' rents did not change, which supports this element. This is what they told you, so it's worth confirming, ideally in writing. It also matters whether their units are similar to yours and whether they are also month-to-month. Your landlord could argue those differences explain the increase.

Probably, if there is a real reason other than your complaint. The statute requires that retaliation be the landlord's primary reason. Your landlord could point to market rates, a unit upgrade, or a different lease type. The timing, three days after the inspection, is strong evidence for you but does not decide the question. The statute also requires that you acted "in good faith." Nothing you've told me suggests otherwise, since the mold is not something you caused.

Whether you can do that is unsettled in this text, so I can't promise it.

Under s. 83.64(3), the protection does not apply if your landlord proves an eviction is "for good cause," such as nonpayment of rent. If you stop paying or underpay, your landlord could call that good cause. I'm not advising you either way. It is a risk to know about.

Whether your landlord has already lost the right to keep any of your deposit is not settled. The deposit is still yours unless the landlord makes a proper claim against it in time. If the window runs from the day you moved out, it has closed, and the landlord must return the full $1,050. If it runs from the lease's end date, the landlord still has time to send a claim.

DETAILS

### Did you give the landlord the notice the law requires when leaving early?
Yes. You left before the lease's July 31, 2026 end date. In that case you must give "at least 7 days' written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating," and the notice "must include the address where the tenant may be reached" (83.49(5)). You handed your letter to the office on April 2, and it included your new address. The last day to give that notice was 2026-04-08, so you were on time. Lease §7 also allows hand delivery to the office. Even if you had missed this step, it would only excuse the landlord from sending a claim notice. ### Did the landlord send a proper claim notice?
No. The landlord must send a written claim notice "by certified mail to the tenant's last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505" (83.49(3)(a)). You told me you received nothing by any means. Your lease also says the parties did not agree to e-mail notices (lease §8).

### Has the 30-day window closed?
This is the open point. The law says that if the landlord does not give the required notice within 30 days, the landlord "forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit" (83.49(3)(a)). The statute does not say whether those 30 days count from the day you moved out or from the lease's end date. Both readings are possible:
- **Move-out date.** The notice to tenants says the landlord must give notice "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)). Counting from April 15, the 30 days ended 2026-05-15, which has passed. On this reading the landlord lost any claim and must return the full $1,050.
- **Lease end date.** The rule begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement," and it speaks of 30 days "after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). It names vacating and termination as two things. If the agreement ended on July 31, 2026, the 30 days end 2026-08-30, which has not passed. On this reading the landlord can still send a claim notice.
- **Your own letters.** The law lets you end the lease if the landlord does not fix a problem within 7 days of your written notice (83.56(1)). A landlord who intends no claim must return the deposit "within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). Counting from April 15, that date was 2026-04-30. Missing it forfeits nothing while the 30-day window is still open.

### Does Florida's landlord-tenant law cover you?
Yes. You confirmed this is a private apartment complex, not tied to any school. It is a unit in a larger building.

### Is the garage space something your landlord has to provide?
Yes, because your lease promises it. Lease §11 says: "Rent includes one reserved space in the covered, gated garage behind the building, space number 12."

That section covers things like structure, plumbing, and codes. A promised parking space isn't in it. Unpaid rent could therefore be treated as plain nonpayment.

### Can you end the lease?
Possibly. Section 83.56(1) says: "If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement."

- **A lease promise the landlord isn't keeping:** Yes. Whether this failure is "material" is not settled. One reading is that any failure to keep a lease promise is material. Your loss is the value of the space you pay for but can't use, plus any real costs, such as street-parking fees. The amount and the court steps are outside this tool.

Your May payment may also affect your right to sue, with the same two readings as above (83.56(5)(a)). The winner of a suit may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). Amounts and court steps are outside this tool.

### Is there a rent reduction built into the statute?
Only in a narrow case. If the landlord's failure is due to causes beyond its control, and it is making every reasonable effort to fix it, 83.56(1)(b) says that if you stay, "the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value." Here the landlord chose and ordered the repaving. Whether that counts as beyond its control is open. I also don't know what efforts it has made to reopen the garage. That is why I asked about what the landlord has said or done. The statute is also unclear on whether this reduction applies automatically or needs agreement between you and the landlord (83.56(1)).

### What protects you if you complain?
A landlord may not raise your rent, cut services, or start an eviction or other civil action primarily to retaliate against you for acting in good faith, for example by sending a notice under 83.56(1) (83.64(1)). A landlord can still act for good cause, such as unpaid rent (83.64(3)).

**Short answer:** The law does not cut your rent automatically, and the lease has no clause that does. Your reserved space is a promise in your lease, so you may have a claim for damages. You may also be able to end the lease, but only after a specific written notice. Please don't hold back rent over this. The rent-withholding rule covers only the repairs in section 83.51(1), and parking is not one of them. Whether a court would reduce your rent for the closure is not settled, because the statute's rent-reduction rule applies to causes beyond the landlord's control. Your landlord ordered the repaving itself.

What have the landlord or the office said or done about the garage since April 15? For example, is repaving work visibly going on, or has anyone given a reopening date?

DETAILS

### Is the parking space something the lease promises?
Yes. Lease §11 says: "Rent includes one reserved space in the covered, gated garage behind the building, space number 12." Nothing in the lease lets the landlord close the garage, and nothing reduces the rent if it closes. Lease §10 says the lease "may be changed only in writing signed by Landlord and Tenant." You did not mention signing anything like that.

### Does your rent go down automatically?
No. Nothing in the lease or in the statute I have read reduces rent on its own. The only rent-reduction rule is §83.56(1)(b). It applies when the failure is "due to causes beyond the landlord's control" and the landlord keeps making every reasonable effort to fix it. In that case, "the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance."
- It is not settled whether that rule applies here. The landlord chose the repaving, which suggests the cause was within its control. The landlord may say the work is necessary and it is moving as fast as it can. What it has said and done will matter.
- Even if that rule applies, §83.56(1) says the lease "may be terminated or altered by the parties." It is not settled whether that means both sides must agree, or whether the reduction applies once the facts are met. I can't pick one reading.

### Can you hold back rent?
I advise against it. Withholding rent can lead to an eviction case. The withholding defense in §83.60(1)(b) covers only "a material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1)." That section covers building codes, structure, and plumbing. A parking promise is in neither list, so it is a lease promise only. If you stop paying, you would have no defense to an eviction case for unpaid rent based on this.

### Can you end the lease?
Possibly, under §83.56(1). The landlord must "materially fail" to comply with "material provisions of the rental agreement," and a written notice must come first. Here is how your facts line up:
- **A lease promise the landlord has not kept:** The garage space is a lease promise, and it has been closed since April 10, with no date to reopen.
- **Whether the failure is "material":** The statute does not define "material," so this is not settled. One reading is that any failure of a lease promise counts. The other is that it depends on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects your life there. You have been parking on the street for over a month.
- **Written notice:** What you described was a question asked in person on April 15. That is not this notice. The notice must be in writing, name the problem, and say you intend to end the lease because of it (§83.56(1)). It must be delivered by mail or by handing over a true copy (§83.56(4)). Lease §7 says to hand-deliver it to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, or send it there by certified mail. Lease §8 says the parties have not agreed to e-mail notices, so e-mail would not count under §83.505(1).
- **Seven days:** The landlord has 7 days after the notice is delivered to fix the problem. I can give you the exact date once you tell me the delivery date.
- **Rent paid with knowledge:** You paid May rent on May 1 knowing the garage was closed. Under §83.56(5)(a), paying rent "with actual knowledge of a noncompliance" waives the right to end the lease "for that noncompliance," "but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." It is not settled which way this cuts. One reading is that a garage that is still closed is a continuing noncompliance, so your payment gave up nothing. The other is that paying with knowledge gave up the right over this closure. Each rent payment you make while the garage stays closed adds to that risk.

### Can you recover money?
Possibly. Section 83.55 says: "If either the landlord or the tenant fails to comply with the requirements of the rental agreement or this part, the aggrieved party may recover the damages caused by the noncompliance." No notice is required first. Your May rent payment may also affect your "right … to bring a civil action for that noncompliance" (§83.56(5)(a)), with the same two readings as above. The amount you could recover is outside this tool. Under §83.48, the winner in a suit may recover attorney fees and court costs, so a suit carries risk for you too.

### Are you protected if the landlord retaliates?
Yes, within limits. Section 83.64(1) makes it unlawful for a landlord to raise rent, cut services, or bring or threaten an eviction case "primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." A notice under §83.56(1) is one of the protected acts (§83.64(1)(c)). You must act in good faith, and the landlord can still defend by proving good cause (§83.64(3)).
